Tell your doctor and pharmacist about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
Medicines that need particular care:
Lithium.
Lithium and diuretics generally should not be taken together.
Hydrochlorothiazide reduces how quickly the kidneys clear lithium.
This reduction carries a high risk of lithium toxicity.
Cholestyramine and colestipol.
These cholesterol-lowering resins bind hydrochlorothiazide in the gut.
They can reduce how much you absorb by up to 85 percent for cholestyramine and 43 percent for colestipol.
The doses need to be separated.
The label advises taking hydrochlorothiazide for the oral suspension.
The label advises taking hydrochlorothiazide at least 4 hours before the resin.
The label advises taking hydrochlorothiazide 4 to 6 hours after the resin.
NSAIDs such as ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), diclofenac, meloxicam, indomethacin, celecoxib and aspirin.
These can reduce the fluid-clearing and blood-pressure-lowering effects of hydrochlorothiazide.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydrochlorothiazide
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug decreases or lessens the severity or occurrence of the condition or function specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Fluid and salt imbalance:
Hydrochlorothiazide can lower the levels of potassium, sodium, magnesium and chloride in your blood.
Low potassium (hypokalemia) is the most common of these.
It is more likely at higher doses.
It is more likely during rapid fluid loss.
It is more likely if you have severe cirrhosis.
It is more likely after long-term use.
Your doctor will check your blood before you start and at intervals during treatment.
Contact your doctor if you have any of the following, which can be signs of a fluid or salt imbalance:
dry mouth, thirst, or unusual weakness or tiredness
drowsiness, restlessness or confusion
muscle pain, cramps or muscle fatigue
fast heartbeat
passing much less urine than usual
nausea or vomiting
seizures
Kidney and liver problems:
HCTZ reduces the fluid volume in your body.
This reduction can lead to sudden kidney injury.
The risk is higher if you have chronic kidney disease.
The risk is higher if you have heart failure.
The risk is higher if you are already low on fluid.

congestive heart failure

Tell your doctor about all your medical conditions.
Tell your doctor about all your medications.
Do this before starting fluoxetine (Prozac).
Some medical conditions may interact with fluoxetine.
Some medications may interact with fluoxetine.
Some conditions or medications may affect whether fluoxetine is safe for you.
Tell your doctor if you take any of the following medications or supplements:
Triptans (for migraine)
Antidepressants or mood stabilizers, including SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, MAOIs, lithium, buspirone, or antipsychotics
Amphetamines
Opioid pain medications, including tramadol, fentanyl, meperidine, or methadone
Over-the-counter supplements such as St. John's Wort or tryptophan
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
Many of these combinations can increase the risk of serotonin syndrome.
Serotonin syndrome is a potentially serious condition.
Tell your doctor if you have or have had any of the following:
Liver, kidney, or heart problems
Seizures or epilepsy
Bipolar disorder or mania
Low sodium levels in the blood
A stroke or high blood pressure
Bleeding problems
Pregnancy

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Fluoxetine (Prozac) is taken orally.
Your doctor will determine the right dose for you based on your condition, age, and response to treatment.
Always follow your doctor's instructions.
Do not change your dose or stop taking this medicine without speaking to them first.
Major Depressive Disorder (MDD):
Adults: Treatment typically starts at 20 mg once daily in the morning.
Your doctor may increase the dose after several weeks if needed.
The maximum dose is 80 mg/day.
Children and adolescents (aged 8 and older): Treatment starts at 10 mg or 20 mg per day.
In lower-weight children, the starting dose and target dose may remain at 10 mg/day.
With all patients, the full effect of fluoxetine for depression may take 4 weeks or longer.
Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD):
Adult dose: Treatment starts at 20 mg once daily in the morning.
It may be increased after several weeks if there is a lack of clinical improvement.
The recommended dose range is 20 mg to 60 mg per day.
Full therapeutic effect may take 5 weeks or longer.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
How long does fluoxetine take to work?
:
Most people need to take fluoxetine for 4 to 6 weeks before feeling the full effects.
Some improvement in sleep, appetite, or energy levels may be noticeable within the first 1 to 2 weeks.
Mood and motivation typically take longer to improve.
For obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), it may take 5 weeks or longer to see the full benefit.
It is important to keep taking this medicine as prescribed.
You should continue even if you do not feel immediate improvement.
Do not stop without speaking to your doctor first.
Is fluoxetine a controlled substance?
:
No, fluoxetine is not a controlled substance.
It is not classified under the DEA Controlled Substances Act.
This means it does not have recognized potential for dependence or abuse.
Drugs like opioids or benzodiazepines have this potential.
It is, however, a prescription-only medicine.
It still requires a valid prescription from a licensed healthcare provider.
Is fluoxetine an SSRI?
:
Yes, fluoxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI).

graph_edge.subject: Fluoxetine
graph_edge.object: increased risk of suicidal thoughts in children, adolescents, and young adults
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Like all medications, Prozac carries some important warnings you should be aware of before and during treatment.
Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following.
Boxed warning:
Fluoxetine carries a boxed warning, the FDA's most serious warning, regarding suicidal thoughts and behavior.
Antidepressants may increase the risk of suicidal thoughts in children, adolescents, and young adults.
Fluoxetine is an antidepressant.
The risk is particularly high in the first few months of treatment.
The risk is also high when the dose is changed.
This risk was not seen in adults over 24.
Adults 65 and older actually showed a reduced risk.
Anyone starting this medicine should be closely monitored for worsening mood or new or worsening suicidal thoughts.
Families and caregivers should stay in regular contact with the prescriber.
Other warnings:
Serotonin syndrome: A potentially life-threatening condition that can occur when serotonin builds up to dangerous levels.
This can occur when taken alone.
It is more likely when taken with other serotonergic medications.

How long does fluoxetine take to work?
:
Most people need to take fluoxetine for 4 to 6 weeks before feeling the full effects.
Some improvement in sleep, appetite, or energy levels may be noticeable within the first 1 to 2 weeks.
Mood and motivation typically take longer to improve.
For obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), it may take 5 weeks or longer to see the full benefit.
It is important to keep taking this medicine as prescribed.
You should continue even if you do not feel immediate improvement.
Do not stop without speaking to your doctor first.
Is fluoxetine a controlled substance?
:
No, fluoxetine is not a controlled substance.
It is not classified under the DEA Controlled Substances Act.
This means it does not have recognized potential for dependence or abuse.
Drugs like opioids or benzodiazepines have this potential.
It is, however, a prescription-only medicine.
It still requires a valid prescription from a licensed healthcare provider.
Is fluoxetine an SSRI?
:
Yes, fluoxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI).

Tell your doctor about all your medical conditions.
Tell your doctor about all your medications.
Do this before starting fluoxetine (Prozac).
Some medical conditions may interact with fluoxetine.
Some medications may interact with fluoxetine.
Some conditions or medications may affect whether fluoxetine is safe for you.
Tell your doctor if you take any of the following medications or supplements:
Triptans (for migraine)
Antidepressants or mood stabilizers, including SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, MAOIs, lithium, buspirone, or antipsychotics
Amphetamines
Opioid pain medications, including tramadol, fentanyl, meperidine, or methadone
Over-the-counter supplements such as St. John's Wort or tryptophan
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
Many of these combinations can increase the risk of serotonin syndrome.
Serotonin syndrome is a potentially serious condition.
Tell your doctor if you have or have had any of the following:
Liver, kidney, or heart problems
Seizures or epilepsy
Bipolar disorder or mania
Low sodium levels in the blood
A stroke or high blood pressure
Bleeding problems
Pregnancy

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Using fluoxetine with other drugs that make you drowsy can worsen this effect.
Ask your doctor before using opioid medication, a sleeping pill, a muscle relaxer, or medicine for anxiety or seizures.
Ask your doctor before taking a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) such as aspirin, ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), celecoxib (Celebrex), diclofenac, indomethacin, meloxicam, and others.
Using an NSAID with fluoxetine may cause you to bruise or bleed easily.
Fluoxetine can cause a serious heart problem.
Your risk of this heart problem may be higher if you also use certain other medicines.
These other medicines are used for infections.
These other medicines are used for asthma.
These other medicines are used for heart problems.
These other medicines are used for high blood pressure.
These other medicines are used for depression.
These other medicines are used for mental illness.
These other medicines are used for cancer.
These other medicines are used for malaria.
These other medicines are used for HIV.
Tell your doctor about all your current medicines.

Do not take fluoxetine if any of the following apply to you.
Tell your doctor or pharmacist about all medications you currently take or have recently stopped taking.
Do not take fluoxetine if you:
Are allergic to fluoxetine or any of its ingredients
Currently take a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), including the antibiotic linezolid.
If you are unsure whether your medication is an MAOI, ask your doctor or pharmacist
Stopped taking an MAOI in the last 2 weeks
Currently take pimozide (Orap) as this combination can cause a serious, potentially life-threatening irregular heart rhythm
Currently taking thioridazine (Mellaril) as this combination can cause a dangerous irregular heart rhythm
Important timing rules with MAOIs and thioridazine:
Wait at least 2 weeks after stopping an MAOI before starting fluoxetine
Wait at least 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before starting an MAOI or thioridazine

If drowsiness develops, a reduction of dosage may be necessary.
-This drug should be taken shortly after a meal or light snack.
Use: Treatment of major depressive disorder (MDD)

graph_edge.subject: amoxicillin
graph_edge.relation_definition: The medical condition specified by the subject may present with the symptom specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Common amoxicillin side effects:
Common amoxicillin side effects may include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or rash.
These side effects affected more than 1% of patients in clinical trials.
Serious amoxicillin side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to amoxicillin.
Signs of an allergic reaction to amoxicillin include hives, difficult breathing, and swelling in your face or throat.
Get emergency medical help if you have a severe skin reaction.
Signs of a severe skin reaction include fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, and a red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
severe stomach pain or vomiting (which may be signs of a serious intestinal condition); or
diarrhea that is watery or bloody (even if it occurs months after your last dose).
This is not a complete list of side effects.
Others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may also report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Common amoxicillin side effects may include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or rash.
These side effects affected more than 1% of patients in clinical trials.
Serious amoxicillin side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to amoxicillin.
Signs of an allergic reaction to amoxicillin include hives, difficult breathing, and swelling in your face or throat.
Get emergency medical help if you have a severe skin reaction.
Signs of a severe skin reaction include fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, and a red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
severe stomach pain or vomiting (which may be signs of a serious intestinal condition); or
diarrhea that is watery or bloody (even if it occurs months after your last dose).
This is not a complete list of side effects.

Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.

Fluticasone propionate is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation in the lining of the nose.
Flonase Nasal Spray is used to treat nasal congestion, sneezing, runny nose, and itchy or watery eyes.
These symptoms are caused by seasonal or year-round allergies.
Flonase Allergy Relief is for use in adults and children who are at least 4 years old.
It is available without a prescription.
Children's Flonase Allergy Relief contains the same medicine.
It is also for ages 4 and older.
Flonase Sensimist contains fluticasone furoate rather than fluticasone propionate.
It is approved for use in adults and children 2 years of age and older.
Children's Flonase Sensimist is also for ages 2 and older.
In Flonase Sensimist labeling, relief of itchy, watery eyes applies to ages 12 and older.
The brand-name prescription version of Flonase nasal spray has been discontinued in the United States.
Generic fluticasone propionate nasal spray is still available by prescription.

candidate_edges.subject: Tamsulosin
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is used to treat or manage the disease or medical condition specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Tamsulosin is used to treat the symptoms of an enlarged prostate, also called benign prostatic hyperplasia or BPH.
These symptoms include a weak urine stream.
They include trouble starting to urinate.
They include dribbling.
They include a feeling of not emptying the bladder completely.
They include needing to urinate often or urgently.
They include getting up at night to urinate.
Tamsulosin belongs to a group of medicines called alpha blockers.
It works by blocking alpha-1 receptors in the prostate and bladder neck.
Blocking these receptors relaxes the muscle there.
This improves urine flow and eases BPH symptoms.
Tamsulosin is taken once daily, about half an hour after the same meal each day.
Capsules should be swallowed whole and not crushed, chewed, or opened.
The tamsulosin brand name was Flomax.
Flomax has now been discontinued in the U.S.
Generic tamsulosin is available.
Tamsulosin is not approved to treat high blood pressure.
It is not approved for use in women or children.

:

In rare cases, tamsulosin can cause priapism.

Priapism is a painful erection that lasts a long time.

Tamsulosin is broken down in the body mainly by two liver enzymes, CYP3A4 and CYP2D6.
Medicines that block these enzymes can raise the amount of tamsulosin in your blood.
These medicines can increase the risk of side effects.
The medicines block these enzymes.
Do not take tamsulosin with:
strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as ketoconazole
other alpha blockers, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, silodosin, or terazosin
Use with caution, and tell your doctor if you take:
moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as erythromycin
strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as paroxetine, or moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as terbinafine
cimetidine
warfarin
medicines for erectile dysfunction or pulmonary arterial hypertension known as PDE5 inhibitors, including avanafil (Stendra), sildenafil (Viagra, Revatio), tadalafil (Adcirca, Cialis), and vardenafil (Levitra).
Taking these with tamsulosin can lower blood pressure enough to cause symptoms.
Some of these cautions matter more at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at 0.4 mg.
Your doctor will decide what is right for you.

candidate_edges.subject: Tamsulosin
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is not indicated or used to treat or manage the condition or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Tamsulosin is used to treat the symptoms of an enlarged prostate, also called benign prostatic hyperplasia or BPH.
These symptoms include a weak urine stream.
They include trouble starting to urinate.
They include dribbling.
They include a feeling of not emptying the bladder completely.
They include needing to urinate often or urgently.
They include getting up at night to urinate.
Tamsulosin belongs to a group of medicines called alpha blockers.
It works by blocking alpha-1 receptors in the prostate and bladder neck.
Blocking these receptors relaxes the muscle there.
This improves urine flow and eases BPH symptoms.
Tamsulosin is taken once daily, about half an hour after the same meal each day.
Capsules should be swallowed whole and not crushed, chewed, or opened.
The tamsulosin brand name was Flomax.
Flomax has now been discontinued in the U.S.
Generic tamsulosin is available.
Tamsulosin is not approved to treat high blood pressure.
It is not approved for use in women or children.

graph_edge.subject: Tamsulosin
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug has a drug interaction with the drug or substance specified by the object entity that may change effects or cause harm.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Tamsulosin is broken down in the body mainly by two liver enzymes, CYP3A4 and CYP2D6.
Medicines that block these enzymes can raise the amount of tamsulosin in your blood.
These medicines can increase the risk of side effects.
The medicines block these enzymes.
Do not take tamsulosin with:
strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as ketoconazole
other alpha blockers, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, silodosin, or terazosin
Use with caution, and tell your doctor if you take:
moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as erythromycin
strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as paroxetine, or moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as terbinafine
cimetidine
warfarin
medicines for erectile dysfunction or pulmonary arterial hypertension known as PDE5 inhibitors, including avanafil (Stendra), sildenafil (Viagra, Revatio), tadalafil (Adcirca, Cialis), and vardenafil (Levitra).
Taking these with tamsulosin can lower blood pressure enough to cause symptoms.
Some of these cautions matter more at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at 0.4 mg.
Your doctor will decide what is right for you.

Tamsulosin is used to treat the symptoms of an enlarged prostate, also called benign prostatic hyperplasia or BPH.
These symptoms include a weak urine stream.
They include trouble starting to urinate.
They include dribbling.
They include a feeling of not emptying the bladder completely.
They include needing to urinate often or urgently.
They include getting up at night to urinate.
Tamsulosin belongs to a group of medicines called alpha blockers.
It works by blocking alpha-1 receptors in the prostate and bladder neck.
Blocking these receptors relaxes the muscle there.
This improves urine flow and eases BPH symptoms.
Tamsulosin is taken once daily, about half an hour after the same meal each day.
Capsules should be swallowed whole and not crushed, chewed, or opened.
The tamsulosin brand name was Flomax.
Flomax has now been discontinued in the U.S.
Generic tamsulosin is available.
Tamsulosin is not approved to treat high blood pressure.
It is not approved for use in women or children.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, itching, rash, swelling of your face, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing.
Rarely, tamsulosin has been linked to severe skin reactions with blistering and peeling of the skin.
Stop taking tamsulosin and call your doctor at once if you have:
a lightheaded feeling, like you might pass out
a painful erection that will not go away and is not related to sexual activity
What are the common side effects of tamsulosin?
:
Common tamsulosin side effects may include:
headache
dizziness
runny or stuffy nose, sore throat, cough, sinus congestion
flu-like symptoms or infection
weakness or lack of energy
back pain, chest pain
diarrhea, nausea
drowsiness or trouble sleeping
tooth problems
abnormal ejaculation, including a smaller amount of semen or no semen at all
reduced interest in sex
blurred vision
Some side effects are more likely at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at the usual 0.4 mg starting dose.
In clinical studies, abnormal ejaculation was reported by about 8 in 100 men taking 0.4 mg.

Do not take tamsulosin if you are allergic to tamsulosin or to any of the ingredients in the capsule.
Do not take tamsulosin with other alpha blockers.
Examples of other alpha blockers include alfuzosin (Uroxatral), doxazosin (Cardura), prazosin (Minipress), silodosin (Rapaflo), and terazosin (Hytrin).
Do not take tamsulosin 0.4 mg with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole.
These medicines raise tamsulosin levels in your blood.
Tamsulosin can lower your blood pressure when you stand up.
This may make you feel dizzy or faint.
This is most likely when you first start taking it.
This is most likely when your dose changes.
This is most likely when you start it again after a break.
Get up slowly from sitting or lying down.
Be careful driving or doing anything that needs you to be alert until you know how tamsulosin affects you.
In rare cases, tamsulosin can cause priapism.
These cases probably occur in fewer than 1 in 50,000 patients.
Priapism is a painful erection that lasts a long time.
Priapism is not related to sexual activity.

candidate_edges.subject: Tamsulosin
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The medical condition specified by the subject may present with the symptom specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, itching, rash, swelling of your face, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing.
Rarely, tamsulosin has been linked to severe skin reactions with blistering and peeling of the skin.
Stop taking tamsulosin and call your doctor at once if you have:
a lightheaded feeling, like you might pass out
a painful erection that will not go away and is not related to sexual activity
What are the common side effects of tamsulosin?
:
Common tamsulosin side effects may include:
headache
dizziness
runny or stuffy nose, sore throat, cough, sinus congestion
flu-like symptoms or infection
weakness or lack of energy
back pain, chest pain
diarrhea, nausea
drowsiness or trouble sleeping
tooth problems
abnormal ejaculation, including a smaller amount of semen or no semen at all
reduced interest in sex
blurred vision
Some side effects are more likely at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at the usual 0.4 mg starting dose.
In clinical studies, abnormal ejaculation was reported by about 8 in 100 men taking 0.4 mg.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Do not take tamsulosin if you are allergic to tamsulosin or to any of the ingredients in the capsule.
Do not take tamsulosin with other alpha blockers.
Examples of other alpha blockers include alfuzosin (Uroxatral), doxazosin (Cardura), prazosin (Minipress), silodosin (Rapaflo), and terazosin (Hytrin).
Do not take tamsulosin 0.4 mg with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole.
These medicines raise tamsulosin levels in your blood.
Tamsulosin can lower your blood pressure when you stand up.
This may make you feel dizzy or faint.
This is most likely when you first start taking it.
This is most likely when your dose changes.
This is most likely when you start it again after a break.
Get up slowly from sitting or lying down.
Be careful driving or doing anything that needs you to be alert until you know how tamsulosin affects you.
In rare cases, tamsulosin can cause priapism.
These cases probably occur in fewer than 1 in 50,000 patients.
Priapism is a painful erection that lasts a long time.
Priapism is not related to sexual activity.

They include needing to urinate often or urgently.
They include getting up at night to urinate.
Tamsulosin belongs to a group of medicines called alpha blockers.
It works by blocking alpha-1 receptors in the prostate and bladder neck.
Blocking these receptors relaxes the muscle there.
This improves urine flow and eases BPH symptoms.
Tamsulosin is taken once daily, about half an hour after the same meal each day.
Capsules should be swallowed whole and not crushed, chewed, or opened.

Generic tamsulosin is available.
Tamsulosin is not approved to treat high blood pressure.
It is not approved for use in women or children.

graph_edge.subject: Tamsulosin
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject entity is metabolized by the enzyme or process specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Tamsulosin is broken down in the body mainly by two liver enzymes, CYP3A4 and CYP2D6.
Medicines that block these enzymes can raise the amount of tamsulosin in your blood.
These medicines can increase the risk of side effects.
The medicines block these enzymes.
Do not take tamsulosin with:
strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as ketoconazole
other alpha blockers, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, silodosin, or terazosin
Use with caution, and tell your doctor if you take:
moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as erythromycin
strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as paroxetine, or moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as terbinafine
cimetidine
warfarin
medicines for erectile dysfunction or pulmonary arterial hypertension known as PDE5 inhibitors, including avanafil (Stendra), sildenafil (Viagra, Revatio), tadalafil (Adcirca, Cialis), and vardenafil (Levitra).
Taking these with tamsulosin can lower blood pressure enough to cause symptoms.
Some of these cautions matter more at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at 0.4 mg.
Your doctor will decide what is right for you.

The procedure could be a spinal tap.

Apixaban can make it easier for you to bleed, even from a minor injury.

artificial heart valve;
a history of problems with your spine, a spinal surgery, or difficult or repeated spinal taps;
bleeding problems;
plan for surgery, or a medical or a dental procedure;
a thin tube (catheter) placed in your back to give you certain medicine;
antiphospholipid syndrome, an immune system disorder that increases the risk of blood clots; or
liver or kidney disease.
It is not known if apixaban will harm an unborn baby.
Taking apixaban during pregnancy may cause bleeding in the mother or the unborn baby.

These patients have type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
Basasglar is FDA-approved to be used by adults for type 2 diabetes.
It is also approved for adults and pediatric patients with type 1 diabetes.
In patients with type 1 diabetes, insulin glargine must be used together with a short-acting insulin.

If you use an injection pen, use only the injection pen that comes with insulin glargine.
Attach a new needle before each use.
Do not transfer the insulin from the pen into a syringe.
Never share an injection pen, even if you changed the needle.
Sharing these devices can pass infections from person to person.
Blood sugar can be affected by stress, illness, surgery, exercise, alcohol use, or skipping meals.

Wear a medical alert tag or carry an ID card to let others know you have diabetes.

These symptoms may get worse quickly.
Empagliflozin may cause serious side effects.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out;
low blood sugar -- headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery;
dehydration --dizziness, confusion, feeling very thirsty, less urination;

Common side effects:
Common furosemide side effects may include:
diarrhea, constipation, loss of appetite
numbness or tingling
headache, dizziness
blurred vision
redness, bruising, swelling, or pain where a subcutaneous dose is given.
Serious furosemide side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to furosemide, such as hives, difficult breathing, or swelling in your face or throat.
Get emergency medical help if you have a severe skin reaction, such as fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, or a red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling.
Furosemide may cause other serious side effects.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out
ringing in your ears, hearing loss
muscle spasms or contractions
pale skin, easy bruising, unusual bleeding
high blood sugar, with increased thirst, increased urination, dry mouth, or fruity breath odor
kidney problems, with swelling, urinating less, feeling tired or short of breath

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Take Meloxicam exactly as prescribed by your doctor.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Use the lowest effective dose for your condition.
Meloxicam oral is taken by mouth.
Meloxicam injection (Qamzova, Xifyrm) is given as an intravenous bolus injection over 15 seconds.
A healthcare provider will give you this injection.
Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of meloxicam.
Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes.
Meloxicam doses are based on weight (especially in children and teenagers).
Your dose needs may change if you gain or lose weight.
If you use this medicine long-term, you may need frequent medical tests.
Store oral suspension, tablets, or capsules at room temperature, away from moisture and heat.
Keep the bottle tightly closed when not in use.

Oral Tablets and Oral Disintegrating Tablets have an initial dose of 7.5 mg orally once a day.

The maximum dose is 15 mg orally once a day.

candidate_edges.subject: meloxicam
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The object condition or situation increases the likelihood of the subject condition occurring.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Meloxicam can increase your risk of a fatal heart attack or stroke.
This risk is especially high if you use it long term.
The risk is also higher if you take high doses.
The risk is further increased if you have heart disease.
Even people without heart disease or risk factors could have a stroke or heart attack while taking this medicine.
Do not use this medicine just before or after heart bypass surgery (coronary artery bypass graft, or CABG).
Avoid taking meloxicam after a recent heart attack, unless your doctor tells you to.
You may have an increased risk of another heart attack if you take this medicine after a recent heart attack.
Get emergency medical help if you have chest pain, weakness, shortness of breath, slurred speech, or problems with vision or balance.
Meloxicam may also cause stomach or intestinal bleeding.
This bleeding can be fatal.
These conditions can occur without warning while you are using this medicine, especially in older adults.
Call your doctor at once if you have symptoms of stomach bleeding.
These symptoms include black, bloody, or tarry stools.

candidate_edges.subject: meloxicam
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The object condition or situation increases the likelihood of the subject condition occurring.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Meloxicam can increase your risk of a fatal heart attack or stroke.
This risk is especially high if you use it long term.
The risk is also higher if you take high doses.
The risk is further increased if you have heart disease.
Even people without heart disease or risk factors could have a stroke or heart attack while taking this medicine.
Do not use this medicine just before or after heart bypass surgery (coronary artery bypass graft, or CABG).
Avoid taking meloxicam after a recent heart attack, unless your doctor tells you to.
You may have an increased risk of another heart attack if you take this medicine after a recent heart attack.
Get emergency medical help if you have chest pain, weakness, shortness of breath, slurred speech, or problems with vision or balance.
Meloxicam may also cause stomach or intestinal bleeding.
This bleeding can be fatal.
These conditions can occur without warning while you are using this medicine, especially in older adults.
Call your doctor at once if you have symptoms of stomach bleeding.
These symptoms include black, bloody, or tarry stools.

Hydrocodone and acetaminophen is a strong prescription combination pain medicine.
The medicine contains an opioid, hydrocodone.
The medicine also contains acetaminophen.

It is also used when you cannot tolerate other pain treatments.

Generic hydrocodone and acetaminophen tablets and oral solution is still available.
Hydrocodone and acetaminophen first gained FDA approval on May 3, 1982.

Maximum dose: 90 mL/24 hours

Initial dose: 11.25 mL every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain
Maximum dose: 67.5 mL/24 hours

The titration should minimize adverse reactions.

The duration should be consistent with individual patient treatment goals.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
An overdose of acetaminophen and hydrocodone can be fatal.
Acute overdosage with hydrocodone and acetaminophen can cause respiratory depression.
It can cause sleepiness progressing to near-unconsciousness or coma.
It can cause floppy muscles.
It can cause cold and clammy skin.
It can cause constricted pupils.
It can cause pulmonary edema in some cases.
It can cause a slow heartbeat.
It can cause low blood pressure.
It can cause partial or complete airway obstruction.
It can cause unusual snoring.
It can cause death.
If the patient who has overdosed becomes very low in oxygen.
Pupils may become very dilated instead of constricted.
Your doctor may recommend that you get naloxone.
Naloxone is a medicine to reverse an opioid overdose.
Your doctor may recommend that you keep naloxone with you at all times.
A person caring for you can give the naloxone if you stop breathing or don't wake up.
Your caregiver must still get emergency medical help.

Head injury, seizures
Liver, kidney, thyroid problems
Problems urinating
Pancreas or gallbladder problems
Abuse of street or prescription drugs, alcohol addiction, or mental health problems.

Pregnant or planning to become pregnant.

Breastfeeding.

Severe asthma, trouble breathing, or other lung problems
A bowel blockage or a narrowing of the stomach or intestines
Signs of an allergy, such as a rash
Are allergic to any of its ingredients.
Before taking hydrocodone and acetaminophen, tell your healthcare provider if you have a history of:
Head injury, seizures
Liver, kidney, thyroid problems
Problems urinating
Pancreas or gallbladder problems
Abuse of street or prescription drugs, alcohol addiction, or mental health problems.
Tell your healthcare provider if you are:
Pregnant or planning to become pregnant.

Breastfeeding.
Hydrocodone and acetaminophen pass into breast milk and may harm your baby.
Carefully observe infants for increased sleepiness (more than usual), breathing difficulties, or limpness.
Seek immediate medical care if you notice these signs.

It can cause constricted pupils.
It can cause pulmonary edema in some cases.
It can cause a slow heartbeat.
It can cause low blood pressure.
It can cause partial or complete airway obstruction.
It can cause unusual snoring.
It can cause death.

Your caregiver must still get emergency medical help.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Patients on Tirzepatide 15 mg weekly lost an average of 20.9% or 48.6 lb of their body weight after 72 weeks.
This data comes from the Zepbound Study 1 (NCT04184622).
Placebo patients lost an average of 3.1% or 7.2 lb.
Study 1 was a 72-week trial.
The trial compared Zepbound weight loss with placebo.
The trial included adults with obesity or overweight with at least one weight-related condition.
The trial excluded patients with type 2 diabetes.
Zepbound Weight Loss Results at 72 Weeks by Dose:
Treatment dose | Average % weight loss | Average weight lost | Average starting weight
Zepbound 5 mg | 15.0% | 34.0 lb | 226.9 lb
Zepbound 10 mg | 19.5% | 45.5 lb | 233.2 lb
Zepbound 15 mg | 20.9% | 48.6 lb | 232.8 lb
Placebo | 3.1% | 7.2 lb | 231.0 lb

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
In the Mounjaro prescribing information, SURPASS-1 (NCT03954834) was a 40-week trial.
The trial was in adults with type 2 diabetes.
The adults had blood sugar that was not adequately controlled with diet and exercise alone.
Patients received once-weekly Mounjaro 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg, or placebo.
After 40 weeks, 78% to 85% of adults taking Mounjaro achieved an HbA1c below 7%.
This is compared with 23% of adults taking a placebo.
The average HbA1c change was -1.8% with Mounjaro 5 mg.
The average HbA1c change was -1.7% with Mounjaro 10 mg.
The average HbA1c change was -1.7% with Mounjaro 15 mg.
The average HbA1c change was -0.1% with placebo.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
This approval applies to adults with type 2 diabetes.
It applies to those who are at high risk for these events.
Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist.
It activates two gut hormone receptors.
These receptors help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar.
It works by reducing appetite.
It increases feelings of fullness.
It slows gastric emptying.
It boosts insulin release when blood sugar is high.
It reduces glucagon secretion.
Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe.
It should always be used together with diet and exercise.
Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes.
It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.

Initial dose: 2.5 mg under the skin (subcutaneously) once a week.
After 4 weeks: The dosage should be increased to 5 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Further dose increases may occur after at least 4 weeks on the current dose.
The dosage may be increased in 2.5 mg increments.
Recommended maintenance dose for weight loss: 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly.
Recommended maintenance dose for OSA: 10 mg or 15 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly.
Maximum dose: 15 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Dose of Mounjaro for Type 2 Diabetes (Adults and Children 10 Years and Older):
Initial dose: 2.5 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Additional glycemic control is needed.
Increase the dose in 2.5 mg increments after at least 4 weeks on the current dose.
Maximum dose (adults): 15 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Maximum dose (children 10 years and older): 10 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Comments: The starting dose and escalation schedule are designed to reduce the risk of gastrointestinal side effects.

candidate_edges.subject: Tirzepatide
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug is typically prescribed at the dose or dosing regimen specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Usual Zepbound Dose for Weight Loss and OSA (Adult):
Initial dose: 2.5 mg under the skin (subcutaneously) once a week.
After 4 weeks: The dosage should be increased to 5 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Further dose increases may occur after at least 4 weeks on the current dose.
The dosage may be increased in 2.5 mg increments.
Recommended maintenance dose for weight loss: 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly.
Recommended maintenance dose for OSA: 10 mg or 15 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly.
Maximum dose: 15 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Dose of Mounjaro for Type 2 Diabetes (Adults and Children 10 Years and Older):
Initial dose: 2.5 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Additional glycemic control is needed.
Increase the dose in 2.5 mg increments after at least 4 weeks on the current dose.
Maximum dose (adults): 15 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Maximum dose (children 10 years and older): 10 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Comments: The starting dose and escalation schedule are designed to reduce the risk of gastrointestinal side effects.

Usual Zepbound Dose for Weight Loss and OSA (Adult):
Initial dose: 2.5 mg under the skin (subcutaneously) once a week.
After 4 weeks: The dosage should be increased to 5 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Further dose increases may occur after at least 4 weeks on the current dose.
The dosage may be increased in 2.5 mg increments.
Recommended maintenance dose for weight loss: 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly.
Recommended maintenance dose for OSA: 10 mg or 15 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly.
Maximum dose: 15 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Dose of Mounjaro for Type 2 Diabetes (Adults and Children 10 Years and Older):
Initial dose: 2.5 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Additional glycemic control is needed.
Increase the dose in 2.5 mg increments after at least 4 weeks on the current dose.
Maximum dose (adults): 15 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Maximum dose (children 10 years and older): 10 mg subcutaneously once a week.
Comments: The starting dose and escalation schedule are designed to reduce the risk of gastrointestinal side effects.

In the Mounjaro prescribing information, SURPASS-1 (NCT03954834) was a 40-week trial.
The trial was in adults with type 2 diabetes.
The adults had blood sugar that was not adequately controlled with diet and exercise alone.
Patients received once-weekly Mounjaro 5 mg, 10 mg, or 15 mg, or placebo.
After 40 weeks, 78% to 85% of adults taking Mounjaro achieved an HbA1c below 7%.
This is compared with 23% of adults taking a placebo.
The average HbA1c change was -1.8% with Mounjaro 5 mg.
The average HbA1c change was -1.7% with Mounjaro 10 mg.
The average HbA1c change was -1.7% with Mounjaro 15 mg.
The average HbA1c change was -0.1% with placebo.

Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Methylphenidate may be habit-forming.
Misuse can cause addiction, overdose, or death.
Keep the medication where others cannot get to it.
Selling or giving away this medicine is against the law.
Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of this medicine.

Swallow the mixture right away WITHOUT CHEWING.

Apply the skin patch to your hip area 2 hours before an effect is needed.

Do not wear the patch longer than 9 hours a day.
Avoid exposing the patch to direct external heat sources, such as hair dryers, heating pads, or electric blankets.
Tell your doctor if you have a planned surgery.
Your treatment may also include counseling or other treatments.
Your doctor will need to check your progress on a regular basis.
Your heart and blood pressure may also need to be checked often.
Store tightly closed at room temperature, away from moisture, heat, and light.
Keep your medicine in a place where no one can use it improperly.
Do not keep leftover medicine.
Ask your pharmacist about a drug take-back program.

MAO inhibitors include isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, tranylcypromine, and others.
You should not take this medicine if you are allergic to it or if you have ever had:
a seizure disorder;
an eating disorder such as anorexia or bulimia; or
if you have suddenly stopped using alcohol, seizure medication, or a sedative (such as Xanax, Valium, Fiorinal, Klonopin, and others).
Do not take this medicine to treat more than one condition at a time.
If you take bupropion for depression, do not also take this medicine.
Do not take this medicine to quit smoking.
Do not take this medicine for weight management.
Tell your doctor about all of your medical conditions and the drugs you use.
To make sure this medicine is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Do not use this medicine if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days.
A dangerous drug interaction could occur.
MAO inhibitors include isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, tranylcypromine, and others.
You should not take this medicine if you are allergic to it or if you have ever had:
a seizure disorder;
an eating disorder such as anorexia or bulimia; or
if you have suddenly stopped using alcohol, seizure medication, or a sedative (such as Xanax, Valium, Fiorinal, Klonopin, and others).
Do not take this medicine to treat more than one condition at a time.
If you take bupropion for depression, do not also take this medicine.
Do not take this medicine to quit smoking.
Do not take this medicine for weight management.
Tell your doctor about all of your medical conditions and the drugs you use.
To make sure this medicine is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
a head injury, seizures, or brain or spinal cord tumor;
narrow-angle glaucoma;
heart disease, high blood pressure, or a heart attack;
diabetes;

Doctors generally treat doses from 7.5 mg to 40 mg a day as moderate.
Doctors generally treat doses over 40 mg a day as high.
A dose of 20 mg a day sits in the moderate range.
What matters as much as the number is how long you take it.
Side effects build up over time.

:
Yes.

Prednisone has to be converted by your liver into prednisolone before it can work.
Prednisolone is already in the active form.

Does prednisone cause weight gain?
:
Weight gain is a common side effect of prednisone.

Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water.
Holding onto salt and water adds weight quickly in the first days or weeks.
Prednisone increases appetite.
Increased appetite adds body fat over longer courses.
It also moves fat toward the face, neck, upper back and waist.
Weight from fluid usually goes once you stop.
Weight from extra eating takes longer to shift.

Is prednisone a steroid?
:
Yes.
Prednisone is a corticosteroid, also called a glucocorticoid.
Corticosteroids are copies of hormones your adrenal glands make naturally.
They work by lowering inflammation and immune activity.
They are not the same as the anabolic steroids some athletes misuse to build muscle.
How long does it take for prednisone to work?
:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour.
Many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day.
Some conditions take several days or longer to respond.
Delayed-release tablets are designed to release the medicine about four hours after you take them.
Therefore, the timing of your dose matters.
How long does prednisone stay in your system?
:
Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours.
This means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time.
Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.
The effect lasts longer than the drug itself.
A single dose of prednisone quiets your own adrenal glands.

Taking it, especially later in the day, can leave you feeling wired, restless or unable to sleep.
Taking your dose in the morning often helps.
Talk to your doctor before changing when you take it.
Does prednisone raise blood pressure?
:
It can.
Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water.
This raises blood pressure in some people.
This effect is particularly seen at higher doses or on longer courses.
Your blood pressure should be checked during treatment.
Your doctor may ask you to reduce salt in your diet.
What is considered a high dose of prednisone?
:
There is no official cutoff.
Doctors generally treat doses under 7.5 mg a day as low.
Doctors generally treat doses from 7.5 mg to 40 mg a day as moderate.
Doctors generally treat doses over 40 mg a day as high.
A dose of 20 mg a day sits in the moderate range.
What matters as much as the number is how long you take it.
Side effects build up over time.
Can prednisone make you tired?
:
Yes.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Is prednisone a steroid?
:
Yes.
Prednisone is a corticosteroid, also called a glucocorticoid.
Corticosteroids are copies of hormones your adrenal glands make naturally.
They work by lowering inflammation and immune activity.
They are not the same as the anabolic steroids some athletes misuse to build muscle.
How long does it take for prednisone to work?
:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour.
Many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day.
Some conditions take several days or longer to respond.
Delayed-release tablets are designed to release the medicine about four hours after you take them.
Therefore, the timing of your dose matters.
How long does prednisone stay in your system?
:
Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours.
This means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time.
Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.
The effect lasts longer than the drug itself.
A single dose of prednisone quiets your own adrenal glands.

Is prednisone a steroid?
:
Yes.
Prednisone is a corticosteroid, also called a glucocorticoid.
Corticosteroids are copies of hormones your adrenal glands make naturally.
They work by lowering inflammation and immune activity.
They are not the same as the anabolic steroids some athletes misuse to build muscle.
How long does it take for prednisone to work?
:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour.
Many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day.
Some conditions take several days or longer to respond.
Delayed-release tablets are designed to release the medicine about four hours after you take them.
Therefore, the timing of your dose matters.
How long does prednisone stay in your system?
:
Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours.
This means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time.
Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.
The effect lasts longer than the drug itself.
A single dose of prednisone quiets your own adrenal glands.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Is prednisone a steroid?
:
Yes.
Prednisone is a corticosteroid, also called a glucocorticoid.
Corticosteroids are copies of hormones your adrenal glands make naturally.
They work by lowering inflammation and immune activity.
They are not the same as the anabolic steroids some athletes misuse to build muscle.
How long does it take for prednisone to work?
:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour.
Many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day.
Some conditions take several days or longer to respond.
Delayed-release tablets are designed to release the medicine about four hours after you take them.
Therefore, the timing of your dose matters.
How long does prednisone stay in your system?
:
Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours.
This means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time.
Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.
The effect lasts longer than the drug itself.
A single dose of prednisone quiets your own adrenal glands.

qualifiers.condition: long-term use for months to years

reason: Edges describe osteoporosis as a symptom or risk factor, not fractures as an outcome of long-term use.
reference_evidence: Taking prednisone for months or years raises the risk of osteoporosis and broken bones, muscle weakness and muscle loss, cataracts and glaucoma, diabetes, high blood pressure, Cushing's syndrome (a set of changes caused by too much steroid, including a rounded face and fat around the trunk), and adrenal suppression, where your body stops making enough of its own steroid hormones.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Is prednisone a steroid?
:
Yes.
Prednisone is a corticosteroid, also called a glucocorticoid.
Corticosteroids are copies of hormones your adrenal glands make naturally.
They work by lowering inflammation and immune activity.
They are not the same as the anabolic steroids some athletes misuse to build muscle.
How long does it take for prednisone to work?
:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour.
Many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day.
Some conditions take several days or longer to respond.
Delayed-release tablets are designed to release the medicine about four hours after you take them.
Therefore, the timing of your dose matters.
How long does prednisone stay in your system?
:
Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours.
This means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time.
Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.
The effect lasts longer than the drug itself.
A single dose of prednisone quiets your own adrenal glands.

graph_edge.subject: Prednisone
graph_edge.object: 5 to 60 mg per day in divided doses
graph_edge.relation_definition: The subject drug is typically prescribed at the dose or dosing regimen specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
The usual starting dose of prednisone for adults is 5 mg to 60 mg per day.
This dose depends on the condition being treated and how severe it is.
There is no single standard dose.
Your doctor will decide on a starting dose.
Then, the doctor will lower it in small steps.
The goal is to reach the smallest dose that still controls your condition.
Doses for children are based on the condition rather than strictly on age or weight.
They must be set by a doctor.
Short courses of prednisone for problems such as an asthma flare, gout, or a bad allergic reaction are often given as a short fixed-dose course for a few days.
A dose pack steps the dose down day by day over about six days.
Follow the instructions on your pack exactly, since the number of tablets changes each day.
Prednisone treatment takes one of two shapes.
Some people take it for a few days or weeks.
They do this for a problem that will settle.
Examples of such problems include an asthma flare or a severe allergic reaction.

reference_evidence: The usual starting dose of prednisone for adults is 5 mg to 60 mg per day, depending on the condition being treated and how severe it is.

confusion, hallucinations, agitation, lack of energy;
a seizure;
fast or pounding heartbeats, sudden dizziness (like you might pass out).

headache;
dizziness; or
constipation or diarrhea.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur.

candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
This applies if you have switched to buspirone from another anxiety medication.

This medication can cause false positive results with certain medical tests.

Tell any doctor who treats you that you are using buspirone.

candidate_edges.subject: buspirone
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Do not use buspirone if you have taken an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days.

MAO inhibitors include isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, and tranylcypromine.

candidate_edges.subject: buspirone
candidate_edges.object: drugs that cause drowsiness or slow breathing
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug has a drug interaction with the drug or substance specified by the object entity that may change effects or cause harm.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Taking this medicine with other drugs that make you sleepy or slow your breathing can worsen these effects.
Ask your doctor before taking buspirone with a sleeping pill, narcotic pain medicine, muscle relaxer, or medicine for anxiety, depression, or seizures.
Other drugs may interact with buspirone.
These include prescription and over-the-counter medicines.
These also include vitamins and herbal products.
Tell each of your health care providers about all medicines you use now and any medicine you start or stop using.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:

candidate_edges.subject: buspirone
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The medical condition specified by the subject may present with the symptom specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Get emergency medical help if you have any signs of an allergic reaction to buspirone.
Signs of an allergic reaction to buspirone include hives.
Signs of an allergic reaction to buspirone include difficult breathing.
Signs of an allergic reaction to buspirone include swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
chest pain;
shortness of breath; or
a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out.
signs of serotonin syndrome, such as agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Common buspirone side effects may include:
headache;
dizziness, drowsiness;
sleep problems (insomnia);
nausea, upset stomach; or
feeling nervous or excited.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You may have breathing problems or withdrawal symptoms if you start or stop taking certain other medicines.
Tramadol is broken down by two liver enzymes called CYP3A4 and CYP2D6.
Medicines that block or speed up these enzymes change how much tramadol and how much of its active form are in your body.
Starting one of these medicines and stopping one both shift the balance.
Tell your doctor whenever you begin or finish a course of an antibiotic, antifungal medication, heart or blood pressure medication, seizure medication, or medicine to treat HIV or hepatitis C.
Many other drugs can be dangerous when used with tramadol.
Tell your doctor if you also use:
medicine for allergies, asthma, blood pressure, motion sickness, irritable bowel, or overactive bladder
other opioid medicines
buprenorphine, butorphanol, nalbuphine, or pentazocine.
These opioids work differently.
They can block tramadol's pain-relieving effect or bring on sudden withdrawal symptoms.
So, they are generally not taken with tramadol.
a benzodiazepine sedative like Valium, Klonopin, or Xanax

candidate_edges.subject: tramadol
candidate_edges.object: opioids generally not taken with tramadol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You may have breathing problems or withdrawal symptoms if you start or stop taking certain other medicines.
Tramadol is broken down by two liver enzymes called CYP3A4 and CYP2D6.
Medicines that block or speed up these enzymes change how much tramadol and how much of its active form are in your body.
Starting one of these medicines and stopping one both shift the balance.
Tell your doctor whenever you begin or finish a course of an antibiotic, antifungal medication, heart or blood pressure medication, seizure medication, or medicine to treat HIV or hepatitis C.
Many other drugs can be dangerous when used with tramadol.
Tell your doctor if you also use:
medicine for allergies, asthma, blood pressure, motion sickness, irritable bowel, or overactive bladder
other opioid medicines
buprenorphine, butorphanol, nalbuphine, or pentazocine.
These opioids work differently.
They can block tramadol's pain-relieving effect or bring on sudden withdrawal symptoms.
So, they are generally not taken with tramadol.
a benzodiazepine sedative like Valium, Klonopin, or Xanax

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Do not take tramadol if you are:
are allergic to tramadol, to any of the other ingredients in your product, or to other opioids
have significant breathing problems (respiratory depression)
have acute or severe asthma and are somewhere you cannot be monitored, or where resuscitation equipment is not available
have a known or suspected blockage of the stomach or intestines, including paralytic ileus
have taken a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) in the past 14 days (such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, or tranylcypromine)
are younger than 12 years of age
are younger than 18 years of age and have recently had surgery to remove your tonsils or adenoids.
Seizures have occurred in some people taking tramadol.
Your seizure risk may be higher if you have ever had:
a head injury, epilepsy, or other seizure disorder
drug or alcohol addiction or
a metabolic disorder.
To make sure tramadol is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have a history of:
Head injury or seizures
Problems urinating
Liver, kidney, or thyroid problems

are allergic to tramadol, to any of the other ingredients in your product, or to other opioids
have significant breathing problems (respiratory depression)
have acute or severe asthma and are somewhere you cannot be monitored, or where resuscitation equipment is not available
have a known or suspected blockage of the stomach or intestines, including paralytic ileus
have taken a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) in the past 14 days (such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, or tranylcypromine)
are younger than 12 years of age
are younger than 18 years of age and have recently had surgery to remove your tonsils or adenoids.

a head injury, epilepsy, or other seizure disorder
drug or alcohol addiction or
a metabolic disorder.

Head injury or seizures
Problems urinating
Liver, kidney, or thyroid problems

candidate_edges.object: opioids generally not taken with tramadol
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug carries a safety warning or precaution about the risk or situation specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You may have breathing problems or withdrawal symptoms if you start or stop taking certain other medicines.
Tramadol is broken down by two liver enzymes called CYP3A4 and CYP2D6.
Medicines that block or speed up these enzymes change how much tramadol and how much of its active form are in your body.
Starting one of these medicines and stopping one both shift the balance.
Tell your doctor whenever you begin or finish a course of an antibiotic, antifungal medication, heart or blood pressure medication, seizure medication, or medicine to treat HIV or hepatitis C.
Many other drugs can be dangerous when used with tramadol.
Tell your doctor if you also use:
medicine for allergies, asthma, blood pressure, motion sickness, irritable bowel, or overactive bladder
other opioid medicines
buprenorphine, butorphanol, nalbuphine, or pentazocine.
These opioids work differently.
They can block tramadol's pain-relieving effect or bring on sudden withdrawal symptoms.
So, they are generally not taken with tramadol.
a benzodiazepine sedative like Valium, Klonopin, or Xanax

This includes postoperative pain.
Postoperative pain is pain after surgery.
Tramadol treats pain severe enough to require opioids.
It may be used as an alternative to other forms of pain relief.
Those other forms did not relieve pain well enough or were not tolerated.
Tramadol extended-release capsules may be used by adults.
The adults require around-the-clock treatment of their moderate to moderately severe chronic pain.
The treatment is for an extended time.
Tramadol should not be used in children younger than 12 years old.
It should not be used in anyone younger than 18 years old with other risk factors, such as breathing problems.
It should not be used in anyone who has recently had surgery to remove their tonsils or adenoids.
Extended-release tramadol (Ultram ER) should not be given to anyone younger than 18 years.

graph_edge.evidence_text:
Potassium is a mineral.
Potassium is found in many foods.
Potassium is needed for several functions of your body.
These functions include the beating of your heart.

Potassium levels can be low as a result of a disease.
Potassium levels can be low from taking certain medicines.
Potassium levels can be low after a prolonged illness with diarrhea or vomiting.

Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include hives.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include difficult breathing.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop using this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have:
severe throat irritation;
stomach bloating, severe vomiting, severe stomach pain;
high potassium level - nausea, weakness, tingly feeling, chest pain, irregular heartbeats, loss of movement; or
signs of stomach bleeding - bloody or tarry stools, coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Common potassium chloride side effects may include:
nausea, vomiting, diarrhea;
gas, stomach pain; or
the appearance of a potassium chloride tablet in your stool.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

graph_edge.subject: Potassium Chloride
graph_edge.relation_definition: The medical condition specified by the subject may present with the symptom specified by the object entity.
graph_edge.evidence_text:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include hives.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include difficult breathing.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop using this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have:
severe throat irritation;
stomach bloating, severe vomiting, severe stomach pain;
high potassium level - nausea, weakness, tingly feeling, chest pain, irregular heartbeats, loss of movement; or
signs of stomach bleeding - bloody or tarry stools, coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Common potassium chloride side effects may include:
nausea, vomiting, diarrhea;
gas, stomach pain; or
the appearance of a potassium chloride tablet in your stool.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

graph_edge.evidence_text:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include hives.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include difficult breathing.
Signs of an allergic reaction to potassium chloride include swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop using this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have:
severe throat irritation;
stomach bloating, severe vomiting, severe stomach pain;
high potassium level - nausea, weakness, tingly feeling, chest pain, irregular heartbeats, loss of movement; or
signs of stomach bleeding - bloody or tarry stools, coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Common potassium chloride side effects may include:
nausea, vomiting, diarrhea;
gas, stomach pain; or
the appearance of a potassium chloride tablet in your stool.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

You should not use potassium chloride if you have high levels of potassium in your blood (hyperkalemia).
You should not use potassium chloride if you also take a "potassium-sparing" diuretic.
To be sure potassium chloride is helping your condition.
Your blood may need to be tested often.
Your heart rate may also be checked.
The heart rate can be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG.
An electrocardiograph or ECG is sometimes called an EKG.
The device is used to measure electrical activity of the heart.
This test will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium.
Do not miss any scheduled appointments.
Serious side effects of potassium include uneven heartbeat.
They include muscle weakness or limp feeling.
They include severe stomach pain.
They include numbness or tingling in your hands, feet, or mouth.
Do not stop taking this medicine without first talking to your doctor.
If you stop taking this medicine suddenly, your condition may become worse.
Do not crush, chew, or suck on an extended-release tablet or capsule.

It is used to treat itching from allergic skin conditions.

Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules in 25 mg
There is also a hydroxyzine hydrochloride injection.
It is given into a muscle by a healthcare professional and is never given into a vein or under the skin.
Hydroxyzine is not chemically related to benzodiazepines, phenothiazines, reserpine, or meprobamate.

Hydroxyzine taken by mouth is approved for three uses.
These are the same for hydroxyzine HCl and hydroxyzine pamoate.
Anxiety and tension.
For symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension linked to psychoneurosis, and as an add-on treatment in physical illnesses where anxiety is present.
Itching from allergic skin conditions.
For managing itching (pruritus) caused by allergic conditions such as long-term hives (chronic urticaria), eczema-type rashes, and rashes caused by contact with an irritant.
It is also used for itching caused by histamine release.
Sedation around surgery.
As a sedative given before a procedure (premedication) and after general anesthesia.
The injection is also approved for nausea and vomiting.
It is usually given in hospital or clinic settings.
It should not be used for nausea and vomiting caused by pregnancy.
Hydroxyzine has not been studied for long-term use in anxiety.
Studies have not assessed whether it still works as an anti-anxiety medicine beyond four months.
Your doctor should review from time to time whether you still need it.

candidate_edges.subject: Hydroxyzine

Hydroxyzine is a prescription antihistamine.
It is used to treat anxiety and tension.
It is used to treat itching from allergic skin conditions.
It is used for sedation before and after general anesthesia.
It comes in three oral forms:
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) tablets in 10 mg, 25 mg, and 50 mg strengths
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride oral solution (a syrup) containing 10 mg in each 5 mL
Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules in 25 mg
There is also a hydroxyzine hydrochloride injection.
It is given into a muscle by a healthcare professional and is never given into a vein or under the skin.
Hydroxyzine is not chemically related to benzodiazepines, phenothiazines, reserpine, or meprobamate.

Hydroxyzine taken by mouth is approved for three uses.
These are the same for hydroxyzine HCl and hydroxyzine pamoate.
Anxiety and tension.
For symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension linked to psychoneurosis, and as an add-on treatment in physical illnesses where anxiety is present.
Itching from allergic skin conditions.
For managing itching (pruritus) caused by allergic conditions such as long-term hives (chronic urticaria), eczema-type rashes, and rashes caused by contact with an irritant.
It is also used for itching caused by histamine release.
Sedation around surgery.
As a sedative given before a procedure (premedication) and after general anesthesia.
The injection is also approved for nausea and vomiting.
It is usually given in hospital or clinic settings.
It should not be used for nausea and vomiting caused by pregnancy.
Hydroxyzine has not been studied for long-term use in anxiety.

Hydroxyzine makes the effects of central nervous system depressants stronger.
If you take hydroxyzine with any of the following, your doctor may need to lower the dose of the other medicine.
narcotic (opioid) pain medicines
non-narcotic pain medicines
barbiturates

Your doctor will adjust these doses for you individually.
Care is needed if you take other medicines.
These medicines can affect heart rhythm.
They do this by prolonging the QT interval.
These include:
heart rhythm medicines such as quinidine, procainamide, amiodarone, and sotalol
certain antipsychotics such as ziprasidone, iloperidone, clozapine, quetiapine, and chlorpromazine
certain antidepressants such as citalopram and fluoxetine
certain antibiotics such as azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin, gatifloxacin, and moxifloxacin
other medicines such as pentamidine, methadone, ondansetron, and droperidol
Hydroxyzine does not affect atropine or other belladonna alkaloids.
It is not known to interfere with digitalis.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use this medicine if you have ever had an allergic reaction to allopurinol.
Allopurinol can lower blood cells that help your body fight infections.
This can make it easier for you to bleed from an injury or get sick from being around others who are ill.
Your blood may need to be tested often.
Visit your doctor regularly.
In rare cases, allopurinol may cause a severe allergic reaction.
Stop taking this medicine.
Call your doctor right away if you have painful urination.
Call your doctor right away if you have blood in your urine.
Call your doctor right away if you have burning in your eyes.
Call your doctor right away if you have swelling in your face or throat.
Call your doctor right away if you have skin redness.
Call your doctor right away if you have a rash that spreads and causes blistering and peeling.
Avoid drinking alcohol.
It can make your condition worse.
Allopurinol may impair your thinking or reactions.
Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be alert.

candidate_edges.subject: Allopurinol
candidate_edges.object: read medication guides or instruction sheets
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug should be taken or used in the manner specified by the object entity (for example with food or at a fixed time).
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Take allopurinol exactly as prescribed by your doctor.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Take the tablets with a full glass of water.
To reduce your risk of kidney stones, drink 8 to 10 full glasses of fluid every day.
Do this unless your doctor tells you otherwise.
Take allopurinol tablets after meals to help prevent stomach upset.
Allopurinol injection is injected into a vein by a healthcare provider.
The injection is usually only used if you are unable to take medicine by mouth.
You may need frequent medical tests while using this medicine.
You may need these tests even if you have no symptoms.
Your kidney and liver function may also need to be tested.
Your doctor may change your dose if your kidney function changes.
You may have gout attacks when you first start taking allopurinol tablets.
Your doctor may recommend another gout medication to take with allopurinol.
Keep taking the medicine as directed.
Your symptoms may not improve for up to 2 to 6 weeks.

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to allopurinol.
Signs of an allergic reaction to allopurinol include hives, difficult breathing, and swelling in your face or throat.
Get emergency medical help if you have a severe skin reaction.
Signs of a severe skin reaction include fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, and a red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling.
Seek medical treatment if you have a serious drug reaction that can affect many parts of your body.
Symptoms may include skin rash, fever, swollen glands, muscle aches, severe weakness, unusual bruising, or yellowing of your skin or eyes.
Allopurinol may cause serious side effects.
Stop using this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have:
any skin rash, no matter how mild;
painful urination, blood in the urine;
inflammation of your blood vessels - numbness or tingling, skin rash, fever, headache, body aches, night sweats, weight loss, feeling or weak or tired;

candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use clopidogrel if you have any active bleeding such as a stomach ulcer or bleeding in the brain.
Clopidogrel increases your risk of bleeding, which can be severe or life-threatening.
Call your doctor or seek emergency medical attention if you have bleeding that will not stop.
Call your doctor or seek emergency medical attention if you have blood in your urine.
Call your doctor or seek emergency medical attention if you have black or bloody stools.
Call your doctor or seek emergency medical attention if you cough up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Do not stop taking clopidogrel without first talking to your doctor, even if you have signs of bleeding.
Stopping clopidogrel may increase your risk of a heart attack or stroke.

candidate_edges.subject: clopidogrel
candidate_edges.relation_definition: The subject drug may be unsafe or require medical supervision for patients who have the condition or characteristic specified by the object entity.
candidate_edges.evidence_text:
You should not use clopidogrel if you are allergic to it, or if you have:
any active bleeding; or
a stomach ulcer or bleeding in the brain (such as from a head injury).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
an ulcer in your stomach or intestines; or
a bleeding disorder or blood clotting disorder.
Clopidogrel may not work as well.
This may happen if you have certain genetic factors.
These genetic factors affect the breakdown of this medicine in your body.
Your doctor may perform a blood test to make sure clopidogrel is right for you.
This medicine is not expected to harm an unborn baby.
However, taking clopidogrel within 1 week before childbirth can cause bleeding in the mother.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
You should not breastfeed while using this medicine.

Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Use these medicines exactly as directed.
Clopidogrel can be taken with or without food.
Clopidogrel is sometimes taken together with aspirin.
Take aspirin only if your doctor tells you to.
Clopidogrel keeps your blood from coagulating (clotting).
It can make it easier for you to bleed, even from a minor injury.
Contact your doctor or seek emergency medical attention if you have any bleeding that will not stop.
You may need to stop using clopidogrel for a short time before a surgery, medical procedure, or dental work.
Any healthcare provider who treats you should know that you are taking clopidogrel.
Do not stop taking clopidogrel without first talking to your doctor, even if you have signs of bleeding.
Stopping the medicine could increase your risk of a heart attack or stroke.
Store at room temperature away from moisture and heat.
